clues.title: Sign: Thin Font Signs
text: The numbers on speed signs are written in a thin font.
The font is much thicker on speed signs in Albania.

clues.title: Chevron: Chevrons
text: Montenegro uses black on white or red on yellow chevrons.
Albania uses white on black chevrons.

clues.title: Coverage: Rifts
text: ‘Rifts’ can commonly be seen in Montenegrin coverage, due to poor stitching.
Rifts are also common in Albania, and can rarely be seen in various other countries.

clues.title: Landscape: Mountainous Landscape
text: Montenegro is a small, mountainous country.
Inland mountains are lush and green, while most coastal mountains have distinct exposed, light coloured rock.
Most roads are also only 1 or 2 lanes wide.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Guardrail: Rusty Guardrails
text: Guardrails in Montenegro are often rusted.

clues.title: Bollard: Bollards
text: The most common bollard is white with a red reflector on the front and a white one on the back.
The bollard also has a black top.
These bollards are also found in Slovenia.

clues.title: Landscape: Dry Mountains
text: Dry mountains with a lack of trees are seen around Podgorica, and to the south of it. Vineyards are also commonly seen in this region.

clues.title: Landscape: Durmitor National Park
text: Durmitor National Park can be recognized by a distinct landscape consisting of grassy, treeless mountains with a high-altitude feel.

clues.title: Guardrail: (Rusty) A & B-Type with red reflectors
text: Montenegro is the only Balkan country where you’ll commonly see both A-type and B-type guardrails. Guardrails in Montenegro are often rusted.

clues.title: Plate: Montenegro
text: Montenegro uses the standard European plate with a blue strip, and the Montenegro coat of arms on a red circle. The red circle is visible through the blur.
NOTE: The white section of Albanian licence plates do not have a red circle.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Montenegrin or Serbian
text: Montenegrin is a South Slavic language and the only version of Serbo-Croatian official in Montenegro. However, Serbian is technically the most widely spoken language in Montenegro, ahead of Montenegrin. For the purpose of this map, these two languages might aswell be the same (they are **that** similar). Both Montenegrin and Serbian are officially written either in Latin or Cyrillic, but Latin is by far the more common script used in Montenegro. Road signs are **not** required to use both scripts, only Latin. Montenegrin uses the letters **Ś** and **Ź** which can not be found in Croatian/Bosnian/Serbian.
The Serbo-Croatian word for street is **ulica**/**улица** (like most Slavic languages).

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
